"This is a 36-week singleton pregnancy with a longitudinal lie and breech presentation. The fetal head is palpable in the fundus as a firm, round, ballotable mass, while the presenting part is softer and irregular. The fetal heart is best heard above the umbilicus. I would confirm the presentation and fetal wellbeing with ultrasound and discuss management options according to gestational age."

"Ultrasound confirms a singleton frank breech presentation, with the fetal hips flexed and knees extended. The fetal head is flexed, growth is appropriate for gestation, the placenta is clear of the cervical os and amniotic fluid is adequate. There is no obvious fetal abnormality. I would discuss external cephalic version and the available delivery options."

"Ultrasound demonstrates a singleton complete breech presentation, with both hips and knees flexed. Fetal growth and amniotic fluid are appropriate, and there is no obvious fetal abnormality. I would discuss ECV where appropriate and, if breech persists, counsel regarding planned Caesarean versus carefully selected vaginal breech birth."

"Ultrasound demonstrates a singleton footling breech with one foot presenting below the buttocks. This presentation is less suitable for planned vaginal breech birth because of the increased risk of cord prolapse. I would involve the senior obstetric team and discuss planned Caesarean delivery unless the clinical circumstances indicate otherwise."

"The fetus is in breech presentation with significant hyperextension of the fetal neck. This is an unfavourable feature for planned vaginal breech birth because of the increased risk of head entrapment and birth trauma. I would involve a senior obstetrician and discuss planned Caesarean delivery."

blocks.text: Maternal discomfort, transient fetal heart-rate abnormalities, rupture of membranes, placental abruption, fetomaternal haemorrhage and rarely emergency Caesarean delivery.

subsections.subsection_title: Q13. What are the delivery options for persistent term breech?

blocks.text: Planned Caesarean section or planned vaginal breech birth in carefully selected women; ECV should also have been discussed/offered where appropriate.

blocks.text: "How would you manage a woman with a breech presentation at 37 weeks?"

"I would first confirm the presentation and gestational age, assess maternal and fetal wellbeing and review the antenatal history, including previous Caesarean, fetal growth, placental location and amniotic fluid. I would confirm the breech type and fetal head position with ultrasound.

For an uncomplicated singleton breech pregnancy at term, I would counsel the woman regarding external cephalic version, planned Caesarean birth and, in carefully selected circumstances, planned vaginal breech birth. ECV would generally be offered around 36 weeks in a nulliparous woman or 37 weeks in a multiparous woman, provided there are no contraindications.

If ECV is successful, she can generally continue with usual antenatal care. If breech persists, I would discuss the relative maternal and neonatal risks and benefits of planned Caesarean versus planned vaginal breech birth. Planned vaginal breech birth should only be considered where appropriate selection criteria are met and an experienced team with immediate access to emergency Caesarean and neonatal resuscitation is available." (nice.org.uk)
Planned Caesarean is commonly chosen because it reduces perinatal/neonatal risk, but selected women may consider planned vaginal breech birth with an experienced team. (nice.org.uk)
